stem:
Tatenda Printers is a sole trader in Bulawayo with a year end of 30 June. At 1 July 2025 machinery had a total cost of US\$144,000 and accumulated depreciation of US\$57,600. Machinery is depreciated at 10% per annum on cost, straight line, on a monthly basis.

During the year ended 30 June 2026:
- on 1 November 2025 a new machine was bought for US\$42,000;
- on 28 February 2026 a machine that had been bought on 1 July 2023 for US\$39,000 was sold for US\$30,500, received in the bank.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the accumulated depreciation on the machine sold, up to the date of sale.
parts.explanation: Two full years (2023/24 and 2024/25) at 3,900 = 7,800, plus 8 months of 2025/26 (July to February): 3,900 × 8/12 = 2,600. Total 10,400.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Two full years (2023/24 and 2024/25) at 3,900 = 7,800, plus 8 months of 2025/26 (July to February): 3,900 × 8/12 = 2,600. Total 10,400.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit on disposal of the machine.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 30 June 2026.
parts.explanation: Machines owned all year: 10% × (144,000 − 39,000) = 10,500. Machine sold: 2,600 (8 months). New machine: 10% × 42,000 × 8/12 = 2,800 (November to June). Total 15,900.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Machines owned all year: 10% × (144,000 − 39,000) = 10,500. Machine sold: 2,600 (8 months). New machine: 10% × 42,000 × 8/12 = 2,800 (November to June). Total 15,900.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Prepare the disposal of machinery account.

points.description: Debit: machinery at cost 39,000
Credit: accumulated depreciation 10,400 and bank 30,500
Profit of 1,900 shown as the balancing figure on the debit side, totals 40,900

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Disposal of machinery account**

| Date | Details | US\$ | Date | Details | US\$ |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| 28 Feb 2026 | Machinery at cost | 39,000 | 28 Feb 2026 | Accumulated depreciation | 10,400 |
| 30 Jun 2026 | Statement of profit or loss (profit) | 1,900 | 28 Feb 2026 | Bank | 30,500 |
|  |  | **40,900** |  |  | **40,900** |

parts.explanation: The profit is the debit balancing figure.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the carrying amount of machinery at 30 June 2026.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Tatenda says: "The profit on disposal shows that the machine was a good purchase." Evaluate this statement.

points.description: A profit means proceeds exceeded the carrying amount
It indicates that too much depreciation was charged in earlier years, not necessarily that the machine was a good purchase
The machine's contribution to revenue over its life should be considered; conclusion that the statement is not justified by the profit alone

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The profit shows that the machine was sold for more than its carrying amount, which means that depreciation charged in earlier years was too high. It does not prove a good purchase, because that depends on the revenue the machine helped to earn over its life.

parts.explanation: A balanced answer separates the accounting correction from the quality of the investment.

explanation: This Cambridge Paper 2 style question tests depreciation on a monthly basis, the disposal account and an evaluation of the result on disposal.
hints: The machine is charged for two full years and 8 months of the year of sale.
The new machine is owned for 8 months (November to June).

stem:
The trial balance of Nyasha Stores at 30 September 2025 did not agree. The debit column totalled US\$118,330 and the credit column US\$118,990. The difference was placed in a suspense account. These errors were then found:

1. A credit sale of US\$2,100 was correctly credited to sales but debited to the customer's account as US\$2,010.
2. Insurance of US\$570 paid by cheque was credited to the bank account but no debit entry was made.
3. Rent received of US\$800 was not recorded in the books.

The draft profit for the year was US\$27,400 and the draft working capital was US\$15,900.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Suspense account

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount placed in the suspense account.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Complete the sentence.
parts.explanation: Credits were higher, so debits were short and the suspense account was debited.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify the type of each error.
parts.explanation: 1 unequal debit and credit amounts; 2 one-sided entry; 3 omission (so the trial balance is unaffected).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Prepare journal entries to correct the three errors. Narratives are required.

points.description: Dr Customer 90, Cr Suspense 90
Dr Insurance 570, Cr Suspense 570
Dr Bank 800, Cr Rent received 800
Narratives given for all three entries

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Journal**

| Date | Details | Debit US\$ | Credit US\$ |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | Customer: trade receivables | 90 |  |
|  | Suspense |  | 90 |
|  | *Credit sale of 2,100 debited to the customer as 2,010* |  |  |
| 2 | Insurance | 570 |  |
|  | Suspense |  | 570 |
|  | *Insurance paid by cheque credited to bank but not debited to insurance* |  |  |
| 3 | Bank | 800 |  |
|  | Rent received |  | 800 |
|  | *Rent received omitted from the books* |  |  |

parts.explanation: Errors 1 and 2 are corrected through suspense; error 3 is not.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the corrected profit for the year.
parts.explanation: Insurance is an expense: −570. Rent received is income: +800. 27,400 − 570 + 800 = 27,630. Error 1 does not change profit.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Insurance is an expense: −570. Rent received is income: +800. 27,400 − 570 + 800 = 27,630. Error 1 does not change profit.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the corrected working capital.
parts.explanation: Trade receivables +90 and bank +800: 15,900 + 90 + 800 = 16,790.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: The accountant says: "Now that the suspense account has been cleared, the books are free of errors." Evaluate this statement.

points.description: Clearing suspense shows that the errors which upset the trial balance have been found
Errors that do not affect the trial balance (omission, principle, compensating) may remain, so the books may still contain errors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A cleared suspense account shows that the errors that upset the trial balance have been found. However, omissions, errors of principle and compensating errors do not affect the trial balance, so the books may still contain errors.

parts.explanation: The trial balance has limitations.

explanation: This Cambridge Paper 2 style question tests the opening and clearing of a suspense account and the effect of corrections on profit and working capital.
hints: Credits are higher than debits, so which side is the suspense account on?
Error 3 does not affect the trial balance.

stem:
Rudo Traders in Gweru found that the balance in its cash book at 30 June 2026 was US\$14,860, while the bank statement showed US\$15,884. The following were identified:

1. Bank charges of US\$126 not yet in the cash book.
2. A direct debit of US\$480 for insurance, not yet in the cash book.
3. A direct credit of US\$1,420 from a customer, not yet in the cash book.
4. A customer's cheque for US\$610, dishonoured and not yet in the cash book.
5. Interest of US\$95 credited by the bank, not yet in the cash book.
6. A cheque to a supplier for US\$1,840 was entered in the cash book as US\$1,380.
7. Cheques of US\$3,260 written but not yet presented.
8. A deposit of US\$2,075 not yet credited by the bank.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State whether each item requires an entry in the cash book.

payload.template: Bank charges: {{blank:a}}. Unpresented cheques: {{blank:b}}. Direct credit from a customer: {{blank:c}}.

parts.explanation: Items first recorded by the bank must be entered in the cash book. Unpresented cheques are already in it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the balance in the updated cash book.
parts.explanation: 14,860 − 126 − 480 + 1,420 − 610 + 95 − 460 = 14,699. The payment was understated by 460 (1,840 − 1,380), so the balance is reduced by 460.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 14,860 − 126 − 480 + 1,420 − 610 + 95 − 460 = 14,699. The payment was understated by 460 (1,840 − 1,380), so the balance is reduced by 460.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Prepare a bank reconciliation statement at 30 June 2026, starting with the balance on the bank statement.

points.description: Starts with the bank statement balance 15,884
Adds the outstanding lodgement 2,075
Deducts the unpresented cheques 3,260
Ends with the updated cash book balance 14,699

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Bank reconciliation statement at 30 June 2026**

|  | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Balance per bank statement | 15,884 |
| Add outstanding lodgement | 2,075 |
| Less unpresented cheques | (3,260) |
| Balance per updated cash book | 14,699 |

parts.explanation: The reconciliation ends with the updated cash book balance.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate by how much profit for the year decreases as a result of the items entered in the cash book (items 1 to 6).
parts.explanation: Bank charges 126 and insurance 480 are expenses; interest received 95 is income. Net decrease = 126 + 480 − 95 = 511. The other items affect receivables, payables and bank only.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Bank charges 126 and insurance 480 are expenses; interest received 95 is income. Net decrease = 126 + 480 − 95 = 511. The other items affect receivables, payables and bank only.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Which figure is shown as the bank balance in the statement of financial position?

options.content: The balance on the bank statement
options.rationale: It excludes unpresented cheques and the outstanding lodgement.

options.content: The balance in the updated cash book
options.rationale: Correct: it includes all the business's transactions.

options.content: The cash book balance before updating
options.rationale: It excludes charges, direct debits and other items.

options.content: The difference between the two balances
options.rationale: The difference is explained in the reconciliation.

parts.explanation: The updated cash book balance is used.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Advise Rudo Traders whether to prepare a bank reconciliation statement every month. Justify your answer.

points.description: Yes: errors, unauthorised payments or fraud are found early, and the true bank balance is known
Limitation: it takes time and does not find errors that appear in both records, but the benefit outweighs the cost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A monthly reconciliation finds errors and unauthorised payments early and shows the true bank balance. It takes time and does not find errors in both records, but the benefits outweigh the cost.

parts.explanation: A benefit, a limitation and a conclusion.

explanation: This Cambridge Paper 2 style question tests the updated cash book, the bank reconciliation statement and the effect on profit.
hints: Items first recorded by the bank update the cash book.
Work out the effect of the cash book error before finding the updated balance.

stem:
Tendai Hardware is a sole trader in Harare with a year end of 30 June. The draft trial balance at 30 June 2026 is shown below. The difference was placed in a suspense account.

**Tendai Hardware: trial balance at 30 June 2026**

| Account | Debit US\$ | Credit US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Premises | 84,000 |  |
| Equipment at cost | 49,200 |  |
| Motor vehicles at cost | 28,000 |  |
| Inventory at 1 July 2025 | 11,350 |  |
| Purchases | 180,000 |  |
| Returns inwards | 1,970 |  |
| Carriage inwards | 2,260 |  |
| Wages | 28,750 |  |
| Rent and rates | 7,970 |  |
| General expenses | 9,840 |  |
| Trade receivables | 15,260 |  |
| Bank | 4,830 |  |
| Drawings | 12,450 |  |
| Suspense | 580 |  |
| Sales |  | 284,590 |
| Returns outwards |  | 2,470 |
| Trade payables |  | 13,180 |
| Provision for depreciation: equipment |  | 14,300 |
| Provision for depreciation: motor vehicles |  | 9,800 |
| Loan from DevBank |  | 18,000 |
| Capital at 1 July 2025 |  | 94,120 |
| **Total** | **436,460** | **436,460** |

**Notes**

1. Errors found:
   - rent of US\$960 paid by cheque was credited to the bank account but no debit entry was made;
   - the purchases account was overcast by US\$380;
   - equipment costing US\$3,200 bought on 1 October 2025 was debited to the purchases account.
2. Depreciation for the year: equipment 10% per annum on cost, straight line, on a monthly basis; motor vehicles 25% per annum on the reducing balance (carrying amount at the start of the year). The provisions shown in the trial balance are the accumulated depreciation at 1 July 2025.
3. Closing inventory was counted at cost of US\$15,600. This includes damaged goods that cost US\$2,150 and can be sold for US\$1,250 after repair.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Prepare journal entries to correct the three errors in note 1 and clear the suspense account. Narratives are required.

points.description: Dr Rent and rates 960, Cr Suspense 960
Dr Suspense 380, Cr Purchases 380
Dr Equipment 3,200, Cr Purchases 3,200
Narratives given and the suspense account clears to nil

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Journal**

| Date | Details | Debit US\$ | Credit US\$ |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | Rent and rates | 960 |  |
|  | Suspense |  | 960 |
|  | *Rent paid by cheque credited to bank but not debited to rent* |  |  |
| 2 | Suspense | 380 |  |
|  | Purchases |  | 380 |
|  | *Purchases account overcast by 380* |  |  |
| 3 | Equipment at cost | 3,200 |  |
|  | Purchases |  | 3,200 |
|  | *Equipment bought on 1 October 2025 wrongly debited to purchases* |  |  |

parts.explanation: Errors 1 and 2 are corrected through suspense; error 3 is an error of principle.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the depreciation charge for equipment for the year

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the depreciation charge for motor vehicles for the year

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: the value of closing inventory at 30 June 2026
parts.explanation: Damaged goods are valued at the lower of cost (2,150) and net realisable value (1,250): write down 900. 15,600 − 900 = 14,700.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Damaged goods are valued at the lower of cost (2,150) and net realisable value (1,250): write down 900. 15,600 − 900 = 14,700.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate, for the year ended 30 June 2026:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: cost of sales

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: gross profit

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: profit for the year

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Prepare the statement of profit or loss of Tendai Hardware for the year ended 30 June 2026, showing the calculation of cost of sales.

points.description: Heading with business name, statement and date; revenue after returns inwards 282,620
Cost of sales calculation including carriage inwards and returns outwards
Gross profit and the expenses including both depreciation charges (own figures)
Total expenses and profit for the year

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Tendai Hardware: statement of profit or loss for the year ended 30 June 2026**

|  | US\$ | US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue (284,590 − 1,970) |  | 282,620 |
| Opening inventory | 11,350 |  |
| Purchases | 176,420 |  |

parts.explanation: The corrected figures are used throughout.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: At 30 June 2026:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: calculate the total carrying amount of non-current assets

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: calculate total current assets

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: calculate the capital of the owner
parts.explanation: Opening capital 94,120 + profit 52,530 − drawings 12,450 = 134,200.

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: prepare the statement of financial position

points.description: Heading and non-current assets with cost, accumulated depreciation and carrying amount (own figures)
Current assets, with inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value
Equity with profit and drawings, the loan and trade payables; totals agree

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Tendai Hardware: statement of financial position at 30 June 2026**

|  | Cost US\$ | Depreciation US\$ | Carrying amount US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Non-current assets |  |  |  |

| Current liability: trade payables |  |  | 13,180 |
| Total equity and liabilities |  |  | 165,380 |

parts.explanation: The statement balances at 165,380.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Analysis

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the gross profit margin for the year, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Gross profit 109,760 ÷ revenue 282,620 × 100 = 38.8%.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Tendai suggests valuing the damaged goods at cost to keep profit higher. Advise him, justifying your answer.

points.description: Inventory must be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (IAS 2)
Valuing the damaged goods at cost would overstate inventory and profit by 900
Recommend writing the goods down; prudence and a fair view

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He should not value the goods at cost. IAS 2 requires inventory to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so the damaged goods are valued at 1,250. Using cost would overstate inventory and profit by 900 and would break the prudence concept, so the write-down should be made.

parts.explanation: The recommendation is supported by the standard and the amount involved.

explanation: This Cambridge Paper 2 style question combines error correction through suspense, depreciation, inventory valuation, the financial statements and an advice part.
hints: Opening suspense is a debit; each correction clears part of it.
Cost of sales uses the corrected purchases figure and the corrected closing inventory.
Capital at the year end = opening capital + profit − drawings.
